<reason>Both sides argued at a high level and stayed on the motion, but B built the cleaner decisive path. B's core claim — that every harm CON presses (unmonitored medication, uncontested claim, the 3am hallway) is a harm *inside* treatment, and the disclosure default is what prevents arrival — was stated early, defended under pressure, and never squarely neutralized. B also landed the sharpest single rebuttals: the dependency turn ("the system defines them as dependents to 26; you cannot lean on that structure and then demand they pay their own way"), the observation that suspicion over an unexplained line item carries strictly less information than an EOB, and the closing seizure of A's own concession in [A4.3] that the sickest patients "do not self-refer under any billing regime" — which does real damage to A's concentrated-harm weighing, since it implies confidential billing costs CON none of those patients. A's best move was the opt-in reframe (available vs default confidentiality), which genuinely sharpened the clash and forced B to answer; A also won a residual sub-point on appeals and miscoded claims, which B only ever waved at ("handled as any confidential claim is"). But A never reconciled the fact that its own fallback — confidentiality asserted at intake, no paperwork home — concedes much of the motion's substance while leaving the payer just as blind in those cases, and B's "a right you must invoke inside a system you already fear is designed to fail the fearful; defaults decide behavior" was a strong answer. A's closing rejoinder (the family that noticed is blinded downstream) was a fair recovery but was met in advance by B's safety-planning/duty-to-warn answer and patient-chosen family involvement. A also carried an execution cost: its first rebuttal was clipped for exceeding the cap, truncating its money argument. On weighing, B repeatedly told the judge why access dominates administrative visibility; A's diffuse-vs-concentrated frame was undercut by its own concession.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's closing use of A's concession that the sickest patients never self-refer under any billing regime: it showed CON's concentrated-harm weighing costs PRO none of those patients, while the disclosure default still loses the treatable self-referrer. A's downstream-blindness reply was a real recovery but did not restore the original comparison.</best_rebuttal>
